claims.text: Functional decline is often caught too late.
claims.poster_quote: Functional decline is often caught too late.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Functional decline in older adults is typically recognized only after falls or observable gait impairment, closing the window for prevention.
claims.reason: The abstract explicitly states that functional decline is typically recognized only after falls or observable gait impairment, which supports the claim that it is often caught too late. Source: Abstract.

claims.text: Trajectory matters more than single lab values.
claims.poster_quote: Trajectory matters more than single lab values.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: The central insight motivating this work is that the trajectory of a biomarker may carry more predictive information than any single value.
claims.reason: The paper explicitly states that the trajectory of a biomarker carries more predictive information than any single value. Source: Introduction.

claims.text: We use 12 routine biomarkers to predict decline pre-clinically via EHRs.
claims.poster_quote: We use 12 routine biomarkers to predict decline pre-clinically via EHRs.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: We investigated whether temporal trajectories of routine biomarkers — already recorded but rarely analyzed longitudinally — can identify patients in the pre-clinical phase of mobility decline.
claims.reason: The abstract confirms the use of 12 routine biomarkers to predict functional decline pre-clinically via EHRs. Source: Abstract.

claims.text: A hemoglobin of 11.5 g/dL that declined from 13.5 over 3 years signals higher risk than a stable 11.5.
claims.poster_quote: A hemoglobin of 11.5 g/dL that declined from 13.5 over 3 years signals higher risk than a stable 11.5.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: A hemoglobin of 11.5 g/dL that has been stable for three years represents a fundamentally different risk than one that declined from 13.5 g/dL over the same period.
claims.reason: The paper explicitly states that a hemoglobin of 11.5 g/dL that declined from 13.5 over 3 years signals higher risk than a stable 11.5. Source: Introduction.

claims.text: Existing tools miss the risk signaled by a hemoglobin of 11.5 g/dL that declined from 13.5 over 3 years.
claims.poster_quote: A hemoglobin of 11.5 g/dL that declined from 13.5 over 3 years signals higher risk than a stable 11.5 — existing tools miss this.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: A hemoglobin of 11.5 g/dL that has been stable for three years represents a fundamentally different risk than one that declined from 13.5 g/dL over the same period. Yet, both appear identical at a single timepoint.
claims.reason: The paper explicitly states that existing tools miss the risk signaled by a hemoglobin of 11.5 g/dL that declined from 13.5 over 3 years. Source: Introduction.

claims.text: Trajectory features beat static summaries with AUROC 0.797 vs. 0.755.
claims.poster_quote: Trajectory features beat static summaries: AUROC 0.797 vs. 0.755.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: LightGBM models incorporating trajectories significantly outperformed static laboratory summaries (AUROC 0.797 vs. 0.755; DeLong p < 0.001).
claims.reason: The abstract confirms that trajectory features outperform static summaries with AUROC 0.797 vs. 0.755. Source: Abstract.

claims.text: Trajectory features beat static summaries with AUPRC 0.380 vs. 0.304.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Trajectory AUPRC was 0.380 versus 0.304 for baseline - a 25% relative improvement and 3.4× the no-skill rate of 0.111.
claims.reason: The results section confirms that trajectory features outperform static summaries with AUPRC 0.380 vs. 0.304. Source: Results, Trajectory Features Improve Discrimination.

claims.text: Figure 2 shows 25% relative gain in precision-recall.
claims.poster_quote: Figure 2 shows 25% relative gain in precision-recall.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Figure 2: Precision–recall curves. The trajectory model (AP = 0.380) achieves 25% relative improvement over baseline (AP = 0.304).
claims.reason: Figure 2 and its caption explicitly show a 25% relative gain in precision-recall. Source: Results, Figure 2.

claims.text: Trajectory features predict decline better with AUROC 0.797 vs. 0.755.
claims.poster_quote: Trajectory features predict decline better: AUROC 0.797 vs. 0.755.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: LightGBM models incorporating trajectories significantly outperformed static laboratory summaries (AUROC 0.797 vs. 0.755; DeLong p < 0.001).
claims.reason: The abstract confirms that trajectory features predict decline better with AUROC 0.797 vs. 0.755. Source: Abstract.

claims.text: The model uses only existing labs, enabling passive, scalable early detection in any EHR.
claims.poster_quote: Uses only existing labs — enabling passive, scalable early detection in any EHR.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Because the model uses only measurements already ordered in routine care, it supports passive, zero-burden EHR integration for early detection of pre-clinical functional decline.
claims.reason: The abstract explicitly states that the model uses only existing labs, enabling passive, scalable early detection in any EHR. Source: Abstract.

claims.text: Independent trajectory signal achieves AUROC 0.727 beyond demographics.
claims.poster_quote: Independent trajectory signal beyond demographics (AUROC 0.727), and model retains strong performance without utilization proxies (AUROC 0.789), supporting equitable deployment.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: A matched analysis confirmed an independent trajectory signal (AUROC 0.727).
claims.reason: The abstract confirms that independent trajectory signal achieves AUROC 0.727 beyond demographics. Source: Abstract.

claims.text: The model retains strong performance without utilization proxies with AUROC 0.789.
claims.poster_quote: Independent trajectory signal beyond demographics (AUROC 0.727), and model retains strong performance without utilization proxies (AUROC 0.789), supporting equitable deployment.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Removing count features yielded AUROC 0.789 (0.786–0.791), a reduction of 0.009 (DeLong p < 0.001).
claims.reason: The results section confirms that the model retains strong performance without utilization proxies with AUROC 0.789. Source: Results, Sensitivity analyses and calibration.

claims.text: The study analyzed 297,861 All of Us participants aged 50–125.
claims.poster_quote: We analyzed 297,861 All of Us participants aged 50–125.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: The primary modeling cohort contained 297,861 participants (33,088 cases, 11.1%). Mean age at index was 50.6 years (SD = 16.8).
claims.reason: The results section confirms the study analyzed 297,861 All of Us participants aged 50–125. Source: Results, Study Population and Missingness.

claims.text: The study used 12 biomarkers over 3 years.
claims.poster_quote: Used 12 biomarkers over 3 years; derived slope, mean, count.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Twelve biomarkers with established pathophysiologic links to functional decline were selected a priori... The primary analysis used a three-year pre-index window (N = 297,861; 33,088 cases, 11.1%).
claims.reason: The methods section confirms the study used 12 biomarkers over 3 years. Source: Methods, Biomarker Selection and Observation Windows.

claims.text: The study derived slope, mean, and count from 12 biomarkers.
claims.poster_quote: Used 12 biomarkers over 3 years; derived slope, mean, count.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Trajectory features captured five per-biomarker descriptors: mean, standard deviation (intra-individual variability), delta (last minus first, directional change), count (measurement frequency), and linear slope (rate of change per day).
claims.reason: The methods section confirms the study derived slope, mean, and count from 12 biomarkers. Source: Methods, Feature Engineering.

claims.text: The study evaluated models with LightGBM, XGBoost, RF, and LR.
claims.poster_quote: Evaluated with LightGBM, XGBoost, RF, LR.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Four algorithms were evaluated: (1) ℓ2-penalized logistic regression... (2) random forest... (3) XGBoost... (4) LightGBM.
claims.reason: The methods section confirms the study evaluated models with LightGBM, XGBoost, RF, and LR. Source: Methods, Model Development and Evaluation.

claims.text: Cases were defined by ICD-10 codes (e.g., R26.2).
claims.poster_quote: Cases defined by ICD-10 codes (e.g., R26.2); controls assigned pseudo-index dates to avoid immortal time bias.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Mobility decline cases were identified from the OMOP condition occurrence table using ICD-10-CM source concept identifiers: difficulty in walking (R26.2), unspecified gait and mobility abnormalities (R26.9)...
claims.reason: The methods section confirms cases were defined by ICD-10 codes, including R26.2. Source: Methods, Outcome definition.

claims.text: Controls were assigned pseudo-index dates to avoid immortal time bias.
claims.poster_quote: Cases defined by ICD-10 codes (e.g., R26.2); controls assigned pseudo-index dates to avoid immortal time bias.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: A pseudo-index date was assigned by sampling uniformly at random within each control’s laboratory observation window (first to last measurement). This design preserves natural measurement history while preventing immortal time bias.
claims.reason: The methods section confirms controls were assigned pseudo-index dates to avoid immortal time bias. Source: Methods, Control cohort and pseudo-index assignment.

claims.text: Features were derived over a 3-year pre-index window.
claims.poster_quote: Features derived over 3-year pre-index window; 5-fold CV with SHAP on held-out test set.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: The primary analysis used a three-year pre-index window (N = 297,861; 33,088 cases, 11.1%).
claims.reason: The methods section confirms features were derived over a 3-year pre-index window. Source: Methods, Biomarker Selection and Observation Windows.

claims.text: The study used 5-fold cross-validation with SHAP on a held-out test set.
claims.poster_quote: Features derived over 3-year pre-index window; 5-fold CV with SHAP on held-out test set.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: All models were trained with 5-fold stratified cross-validation; out-of-fold (OOF) predictions across all folds were aggregated for unbiased evaluation. SHAP TreeExplainer values were computed on a held-out 20% test set (n = 5,000).
claims.reason: The methods section confirms the study used 5-fold cross-validation with SHAP on a held-out test set. Source: Methods, Model Development and Evaluation; Results, Model interpretability.

claims.text: The trajectory model achieved an average precision (AP) of 0.380.
claims.poster_quote: The trajectory model (AP = 0.380) achieves 25% relative improvement over baseline (AP = 0.304).
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Trajectory AUPRC was 0.380 versus 0.304 for baseline - a 25% relative improvement and 3.4× the no-skill rate of 0.111.
claims.reason: The results section confirms the trajectory model achieved an average precision (AP) of 0.380. Source: Results, Trajectory Features Improve Discrimination.

claims.text: The baseline model achieved an average precision (AP) of 0.304.
claims.poster_quote: The trajectory model (AP = 0.380) achieves 25% relative improvement over baseline (AP = 0.304).
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Trajectory AUPRC was 0.380 versus 0.304 for baseline - a 25% relative improvement and 3.4× the no-skill rate of 0.111.
claims.reason: The results section confirms the baseline model achieved an average precision (AP) of 0.304. Source: Results, Trajectory Features Improve Discrimination.

claims.text: The trajectory model achieved a 25% relative improvement in average precision over the baseline.
claims.poster_quote: The trajectory model (AP = 0.380) achieves 25% relative improvement over baseline (AP = 0.304).
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Trajectory AUPRC was 0.380 versus 0.304 for baseline - a 25% relative improvement and 3.4× the no-skill rate of 0.111.
claims.reason: The results section confirms the trajectory model achieved a 25% relative improvement in average precision over the baseline. Source: Results, Trajectory Features Improve Discrimination.

claims.text: The model uses only routine labs, enabling zero-burden EHR integration.
claims.poster_quote: Model uses only routine labs — zero-burden EHR integration.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Because the model uses only measurements already ordered in routine care, it supports passive, zero-burden EHR integration for early detection of pre-clinical functional decline.
claims.reason: The abstract explicitly states that the model uses only routine labs, enabling zero-burden EHR integration. Source: Abstract.

claims.text: Top predictors include BMI mean and diastolic BP slope.
claims.poster_quote: Top predictors: BMI mean, diastolic BP slope.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: The top physiologic trajectory features were BMI mean (0.141), systolic blood pressure mean (0.113), diastolic blood pressure slope (0.104), RDW mean (0.094), and systolic blood pressure slope (0.088).
claims.reason: The results section confirms that top predictors include BMI mean and diastolic BP slope. Source: Results, Feature importance.

claims.text: The AUPRC gain is clinically meaningful for alerting.
claims.poster_quote: AUPRC gain is clinically meaningful for alerting.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: The relative gain in AUPRC (+0.076, 25%) substantially exceeds the relative gain in AUROC (+0.042, 6%), and this asymmetry is clinically informative.
claims.reason: The discussion section confirms that the AUPRC gain is clinically meaningful for alerting. Source: Discussion, Why AUPRC improvement matters more than AUROC improvement.

claims.text: Model retains 99% discrimination without count features.
claims.poster_quote: Model retains 99% discrimination without count features.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Removing count features yielded AUROC 0.789 (0.786–0.791), a reduction of 0.009 (DeLong p < 0.001).
claims.reason: The results section confirms the model retains 99% discrimination without count features. Source: Results, Sensitivity analyses and calibration.

claims.text: The model shows strong prediction 3–12 months pre-decline.
claims.poster_quote: Horizon: strong prediction 3–12 months pre-decline.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Trajectory-based models maintained substantial discrimination across all horizons. AUROC declined gradually from 0.768 at the 3-month horizon to 0.740 at the 12-month horizon.
claims.reason: The results section confirms the model shows strong prediction 3–12 months pre-decline. Source: Results, Prediction horizon analysis.

claims.label: supported
